# Experimental Design

The aim of this experiment is to investigate how toxic cyanobacteria affect the quantity, quality, and timing of the emergence of the predator *Chaoborus* via changes in its prey (Figure 1-2) and dissolved toxins. *Chaoborus* is not fed cyanobacteria directly — it is fed *Daphnia* that were themselves raised on one of `r Treatments` diets (Table 1), so that toxicity and food quality can be varied independently instead of always co-occurring as they do in nature. Two diets are "low-quality": each mixes a cyanobacterium with the high-quality green alga *Tetradesmus obliquus* in a `r Phyto_low_quality_food_ratio * 100`:`r (1 - Phyto_low_quality_food_ratio) * 100` ratio by carbon, one with the toxic *Microcystis aeruginosa* and one with the non-toxic *Synechococcus elongatus* — diluted rather than pure cyanobacteria because *Daphnia* cannot be kept dense enough to sustain the experiment on cyanobacteria alone (see `Phyto_low_quality_food_ratio` in [Parameters](3_parameters.qmd)). This isolates the food-quality effect (comparing either low-quality diet against the high-quality diets below) from the toxin effect (comparing the *Microcystis* diet against the *Synechococcus* diet, since both are equally low-quality but only one is toxic). The other two diets are "high-quality," both 100% *Nannochloropsis limnetica*; they are identical except that the 4th treatment has toxins from lysed *M. aeruginosa* dosed directly into the *Chaoborus* jar rather than through the *Daphnia* diet. Because that route bypasses *Daphnia* entirely, it isolates the effect of toxin exposure alone, uncoupled from any food-quality change, and without whatever biodilution or biotransformation *Daphnia* would otherwise apply to the toxin. 


This is realistic in nature compared to the percentage of biomass made out of cyanobacteria, where a bloom is defined as > 50% of biomass constituted by cyanobacteria [@molot2014].

<p align="center"><strong>Table 1.</strong> Diet composition (by carbon) each treatment's *Daphnia* are raised on, before being fed to *Chaoborus*.</p>

| Treatment | *M. aeruginosa* | *S. elongatus* | *N. limnetica* | *T. obliquus* | Toxin route |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `r Diet_names[1]` | `r Diet_Microcystis_fraction[1] * 100`% | `r Diet_Synechococcus_fraction[1] * 100`% | `r Diet_Nannochloropsis_fraction[1] * 100`% | `r Diet_Tetradesmus_fraction[1] * 100`% | Via *Daphnia* diet |
| `r Diet_names[2]` | `r Diet_Microcystis_fraction[2] * 100`% | `r Diet_Synechococcus_fraction[2] * 100`% | `r Diet_Nannochloropsis_fraction[2] * 100`% | `r Diet_Tetradesmus_fraction[2] * 100`% | None (non-toxic) |
| `r Diet_names[3]` | `r Diet_Microcystis_fraction[3] * 100`% | `r Diet_Synechococcus_fraction[3] * 100`% | `r Diet_Nannochloropsis_fraction[3] * 100`% | `r Diet_Tetradesmus_fraction[3] * 100`% | None |
| `r Diet_names[4]` | `r Diet_Microcystis_fraction[4] * 100`% | `r Diet_Synechococcus_fraction[4] * 100`% | `r Diet_Nannochloropsis_fraction[4] * 100`% | `r Diet_Tetradesmus_fraction[4] * 100`% | Lysed *M. aeruginosa* dosed into the *Chaoborus* jar |

Independently of the treatment diets, the stock *Daphnia* cultures that found each day's cohort jars (see [Calculations](4_calculations.qmd)) are kept on a single, untreated diet — 100% *Tetradesmus obliquus*, fed ad libitum — since they are not part of the toxicity/quality comparison and only need to stay healthy enough to keep producing neonates.
